The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F3] to $\lambda$ and each one-step kernel to obtain joint laws $P(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)M(x,dy)$ and $Q(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)R(x,dy)$. For any product-measurable $A$, the section integrals are measurable by [F4]. If $Q(A)=0$, then $R(x,A_x)=0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ by [F5]; intersecting with the conull kernel-domination set gives $M(x,A_x)=0$ there, hence $P(A)=0$. Thus $P\ll Q$.

By [F6], choose a product-measurable density $h=dP/dQ$. On $N=\{h<0\}$, positivity of $P$ gives $0\le P(N)=\int_Nh\,dQ=-\int_Nh^-\,dQ$, so [F5] makes $h^-=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere on $N$. The Borel positive-part map preserves measurability by [F9], so replacing $h$ by $h^+=\max(h,0)$ leaves the density unchanged $Q$-almost everywhere and makes it nonnegative.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a countable measure-determining algebra on $F$ from [F7], containing $F$. For each $B\in\mathcal C$ and $D\in\mathcal E$, the rectangle laws and density identity [F8] give $\int_D M(x,B)\lambda(dx)=P(D\times B)=\int_D(\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy))\lambda(dx)$. Both integrands are measurable by [F2] and [F4] and integrable because their integrals over $E$ are at most one. Uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym densities in [F6] makes them equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere for each fixed $B$.

Intersect the conull sets from step 3.1 over the countable algebra $\mathcal C$. For each $x$ in the intersection, the section $h(x,\cdot)$ is measurable by [F10], so [F11] makes $B\mapsto\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy)$ a measure. Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

derivations.claim: In the multinomial branch, $C_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^N\mathbf 1_{\{J_\ell=j\}}$ and each indicator has conditional expectation $p_j$ by the specified product mass. Linearity of a finite sum gives $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=Np_j$, including the uniform fallback.

In the residual branch, write $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$ and $r_j=Np_j-q_j$. The remainder $R=\sum_jr_j=N-\sum_jq_j$ is an integer. If $R=0$, every $r_j=0$ and $C_j=q_j=Np_j$; if $R>0$, then $C_j=q_j+\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\mathbf 1_{\{K_\ell=j\}}$ with each indicator having conditional expectation $r_j/R$, so $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=q_j+R(r_j/R)=Np_j$.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the same conditional expected-count identity for both schemes in the procedure, completing the assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.

complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: At time zero, the algorithm gives $\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NG_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)\varphi(X_0^i)$, including when the total initial weight is zero. Each $X_0^i$ has law $\nu_0$, so [F6], finite-sum linearity [F7], and the initial Radon–Nikodym identity in [F5] give $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)]=\int G_0\rho_0\varphi\,d\nu_0=\gamma_0(\varphi)$. The finite target integral makes this random variable integrable.

Every time-zero particle path has law $Q_0$. Inductively, resampling copies only paths already present. If $Q_k(A)=0$, its iterated-kernel formula from [F12] and [F13] gives $R_k(x,A_x)=0$ for $Q_{k-1}$-almost every history; propagation therefore avoids $A$ almost surely whenever every previous particle path avoids each fixed $Q_{k-1}$-null set. Thus sampled parent states lie in the proposal-marginal full sets where the kernel derivatives apply. Each initial or kernel derivative has reference integral one by [F5]. If such a nonnegative derivative were infinite on a set of positive reference measure, its integral would exceed every finite bound; hence all these derivatives are finite almost everywhere. The potentials are finite-valued, so all particle weights are finite almost surely.

Write $\mathcal F_{k-1}$ for the previous particle histories and weights. Let $H_k$ be the integral of $\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$ against the algorithm's conditional finite-step transition law. By [F3], the expected number of children from parent $j$ is $N\bar w_{k-1}^j$. Integrating each child's incremental weight and summing these expected counts gives $H_k=\widehat\gamma_{k-1}^N(x_{0:k-1}\mapsto\int G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k))$. This is initially a nonnegative conditional-kernel integral, not yet an $L^1$ conditional expectation.

By [F4], the target integral of the test function inside $H_k$ is $\gamma_k(\varphi)<\infty$. The induction hypothesis makes $H_k$ integrable with expectation $\gamma_{k-1}(M_k(G_k\varphi))=\gamma_k(\varphi)$. Now [F8] supplies its ordinary conditional-expectation version, and [F2] and [F10] identify $H_k$ by its defining event-integral identities. Apply the established identity at $k=t$ to the constant function $\varphi=1$. Then $\widehat\gamma_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t\widehat\pi_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t$, while $\gamma_t(1)=Z_t$, proving the stated normalizer unbiasedness.

$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix observations $y_{1:T}$, a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$,
a prior probability $\pi_0$, and the finite-horizon Feynman–Kac path model in
[[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. Write
$$L_\theta(y_{1:T})=\gamma_{\theta,T}(1),\qquad C=\int_\Theta L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$
Require every prefix normalizer $0<Z_{\theta,t}<\infty$ for $t=0,\ldots,T$
and $\pi_0$-almost every $\theta$, together with $0<C<\infty$; then the
parameter posterior is
$$\pi_y(d\theta)=C^{-1}L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$

For fixed particle count $N\ge1$, let $U$ contain the full output of
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] at $\theta$ and a terminal index
$K\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ drawn conditionally with its final normalized weight.
Let $m_\theta(du)$ be this measurable auxiliary-variable probability kernel and
let $\widehat L_\theta(U)=\widehat Z_T$ be jointly measurable and nonnegative
in $(\theta,U)$. The required interface is
$$\int\widehat L_\theta(u)\,m_\theta(du)=L_\theta(y_{1:T});$$
[[thm-sequential-particle-estimator-is-unbiased]] supplies this identity under
its finite-horizon support and integrability hypotheses. Define the extended
target probability by
$$\widetilde\pi(d\theta,du)=C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)m_\theta(du)\widehat L_\theta(u).$$

Given current $(\theta,U)$, propose $\theta'\sim R(\theta,\cdot)$ and then
$U'\sim m_{\theta'}$. Apply the general Metropolis–Hastings construction
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] to this proposal kernel and target
$\widetilde\pi$. On rejection retain the entire current pair $(\theta,U)$,
including its stored likelihood estimate and selected path index. When $\pi_0$
and $R$ have densities $p_0$ and $r$, and the current extended target density
is positive, the acceptance probability is
$$1\wedge\frac{p_0(\theta')\widehat L_{\theta'}(U')r(\theta\mid\theta')}{p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)r(\theta'\mid\theta)}.$$
Initialize on the extended-target support, where $\pi_0(\theta)>0$ and
$\widehat L_\theta(U)>0$. Proposed zero estimates are rejected. A density-free version uses the
accepted-flow Radon–Nikodym construction in the cited general-state algorithm.

The selected path stored in $U$ is part of the auxiliary state. Refreshing its
estimate after rejection defines the different Monte Carlo within Metropolis
procedure, not this algorithm.

For any nonnegative measurable $\varphi:\mathsf X_{0:t}\to[0,\infty]$ with $\gamma_t(\varphi)<\infty$, define $\widehat\gamma_t^N(\varphi)=\int\varphi\,d(\widehat Z_t\widehat\pi_t^N)$. Then
$$\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_t^N(\varphi)]=\gamma_t(\varphi).$$
In particular, with $\varphi=1$, the product-of-average-incremental-weights estimator in the algorithm satisfies $\mathbb E[\widehat Z_t]=Z_t$. At each time either multinomial or residual offspring resampling may be used. The theorem asserts no unbiasedness for the normalized empirical measure $\widehat\pi_t^N$ by itself.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

and $\pi_0$-almost every $\theta$, together with $0<C<\infty$; then the
parameter posterior is
$$\pi_y(d\theta)=C^{-1}L_\theta(y_{1:T})\,\pi_0(d\theta).$$

For fixed particle count $N\ge1$, let $U$ contain the full output of
[[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] at $\theta$ and a terminal index
$K\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ drawn conditionally with its final normalized weight.
Let $m_\theta(du)$ be this measurable auxiliary-variable probability kernel and
let $\widehat L_\theta(U)=\widehat Z_T$ be jointly measurable and nonnegative
in $(\theta,U)$. The required interface is
$$\int\widehat L_\theta(u)\,m_\theta(du)=L_\theta(y_{1:T});$$
[[thm-sequential-particle-estimator-is-unbiased]] supplies this identity under
its finite-horizon support and integrability hypotheses. Define the extended
target probability by
$$\widetilde\pi(d\theta,du)=C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)m_\theta(du)\widehat L_\theta(u).$$

Given current $(\theta,U)$, propose $\theta'\sim R(\theta,\cdot)$ and then
$U'\sim m_{\theta'}$. Apply the general Metropolis–Hastings construction
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] to this proposal kernel and target
$\widetilde\pi$. On rejection retain the entire current pair $(\theta,U)$,
including its stored likelihood estimate and selected path index. When $\pi_0$
and $R$ have densities $p_0$ and $r$, and the current extended target density
is positive, the acceptance probability is
$$1\wedge\frac{p_0(\theta')\widehat L_{\theta'}(U')r(\theta\mid\theta')}{p_0(\theta)\widehat L_\theta(U)r(\theta'\mid\theta)}.$$
Initialize on the extended-target support, where $\pi_0(\theta)>0$ and
$\widehat L_\theta(U)>0$. Proposed zero estimates are rejected. A density-free version uses the
accepted-flow Radon–Nikodym construction in the cited general-state algorithm.

The selected path stored in $U$ is part of the auxiliary state. Refreshing its
estimate after rejection defines the different Monte Carlo within Metropolis
procedure, not this algorithm.

Under the hypotheses of [[alg-pmmh]], assume the unbiasedness identity there
holds and the evidence $C$ is finite and positive. Then $\widetilde\pi$ is a
probability measure whose parameter marginal is $\pi_y$. With the terminal
index included in $U$, the joint marginal of $(\theta,X_{0:T}^{K})$ is the
posterior $C^{-1}\pi_0(d\theta)\gamma_{\theta,T}(dx_{0:T})$. The PMMH
transition kernel is reversible, hence invariant, for $\widetilde\pi$; its
parameter and selected-path marginals are therefore exact for every fixed
$N\ge1$. This is an invariance result only; it asserts no irreducibility,
uniqueness, convergence rate, or mixing speed.
